This appeal coming on for admission this day, the court passed the following:

It appears that the respondent No.6 is not served.
However, it is clear that respondent No.6 was proceeded ex-parte and he did not appear before the Claims Tribunal.
2. Under these circumstances, service of notice on respondent No.6 is hereby dispended with.
3. I.A. No.6665/2022 has been filed for condonation of delay.
4. According to the appellant, the appeal was filed with delay of 23 days, whereas according to the office, delay is of 113 days.
The award was passed on 17.01.2022 and the appeal was filed on 22.06.2022.

It is submitted by the counsel for the appellant that before filing an application, certain procedural formalities are required to be completed, which took some time and thus, the delay has occurred in filing an appeal.
5.
For the reasons mentioned in the application, the same is allowed.
6. The delay in filing an appeal is hereby condoned.

7. Heard.

10. The appellant has filed this appeal only on the ground that the deceased was a bachelor and therefore, only his mother can be treated to be his dependant, whereas the Claims Tribunal has taken the father and grand-mother of the deceased as his dependants.

11. It is submitted by the counsel for the appellant that it is not the case of the claimants that the father of the deceased was a non-earning member of the family and was surviving on the income of the deceased.

12. Heard the learned counsel for the appellant.

sentences.text: Three aspects need to be clarified.
The first one pertains to deduction towards personal and living expenses.

In paras 30, 31 and 32,
Sarla Verma [Sarla Verma v. DTC, (2009) 6 SCC 121 : (2009) 2 SCC (Civ) 770 :
(2009) 2 SCC (Cri) 1002] lays down : (SCC p. 136) "30.

(2009) 2 SCC (Cri) 1002]

sentences.text:
Though in some cases the deduction to be made towards personal and living expenses is calculated on the basis of units indicated in Trilok Chandra [UP SRTC v. Trilok Chandra, (1996) 4 SCC 362],
the general practice is to apply standardised deductions.

entities.text: Trilok Chandra [UP SRTC v. Trilok Chandra, (1996) 4 SCC 362]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Having considered several subsequent decisions of this Court, we are of the view that where the deceased was married, the deduction towards personal and living expenses of the deceased, should be one-third (1/3rd) where the number of dependent family members is 2 to 3, one- fourth (1/4th) where the number of dependent family members is 4 to 6, and one-fifth (1/5th) where the number of dependent family members exceeds six.
31.
Where the deceased was a bachelor and the claimants are the parents, the deduction follows a different principle.

In regard to bachelors, normally, 50% is deducted as personal and living United India Insurance Company Limited vs Smt. Saroj on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106024819/
3 expenses, because it is assumed that a bachelor would tend to spend more on himself.

sentences.text: Even otherwise, there is also the possibility of his getting married in a short time, in which event the contribution to the parent(s) and siblings is likely to be cut drastically.
Further, subject to evidence to the contrary, the father is likely to have his own income and will not be considered as a dependant and the mother alone will be considered as a dependant.

In the absence of evidence to the contrary,
brothers and sisters will not be considered as dependants, because they will either be independent and earning, or married, or be dependent on the father.

32. Thus even if the deceased is survived by parents and siblings, only the mother would be considered to be a dependant, and 50% would be treated as the personal and living expenses of the bachelor and 50% as the contribution to the family.

However, where the family of the bachelor is large and dependent on the income of the deceased, as in a case where he has a widowed mother and large number of younger non-earning sisters or brothers, his personal and living expenses may be restricted to one-third and contribution to the family will be taken as two-third.""
14. Thus, in a case of a bachelor, his mother can be treated as his dependant.
Generally, a father cannot be treated as a dependant on a bachelor unless and until it is proved that the father was a non-earning member of the family.
The appellant No.2 Shankar is aged about 50 years and thus, it cannot be said that he was not an earning member of the family.
Even otherwise, there is nothing on record to show that the father of the deceased was a non-earning member of the family.
Accordingly, it is held that only the appellant No.1 was dependant upon the deceased.
